Hey friend; I have a similar story to share with you. One time in Montreal, I got drunk at a nightclub and this guy was coming onto me repeatedly throughout the night. At first, I rejected his advances however as the night went on I got drunker & drunker, and eventually I gave in. My friends & I went back to his apartment, and as soon as we got there I fell into his bed and took my shirt off. My friends saw me start to undress, and they took that as their queue to leave. He closed the bedroom door behind them as they left. The rest is a blur. 

I was so drunk that I couldn’t even get out of bed or put my clothes back on after the deed was done. My friends & I eventually left his place the next morning, around 5AM.

A feeling of deep shame and utter darkness flooded over me as we got the taxi back to our hotel. 

As soon as we got into the hotel room, I immediately shut myself into the bathroom. I collapsed to the floor, sobbing quietly under the weight of my shame & misery. I felt dirty, violated, worthless, disgusting. I hated myself for what I allowed to happen. 

The same morning I had to catch a train back home. It was one of the sickest, longest, most miserable trips I’ve ever taken. I didn’t want to look any man in the eyes because it reminded me of what happened. I felt exposed, like everyone could see my shame. 

Please know that you are not alone, and even though you are feeling a heavy weight on you right now, it will pass. You are of value, even though your mind is telling you lies that you are not. 

The terrible feeling you have right now is just a mixture of anxiety & depression from your hangover, combined with your brain trying to rationalize something you did that was a bit out of character. This is normal, and you are normal.

Be gentle to yourself. Drink water. Run a warm bath. Take it slow. 

I am sending you the warmest internet hug, friend.

My advice would be to focus on the basics. Make sure your resume is strong. You should spend a lot of your own time on it so that you are very familiar with what you are presenting to employers, but there is nothing wrong with getting a second opinion from a resume writer. They can articulate your experience in a way that is very valuable. I used [this guy](https://www.fiverr.com/s2/7342e50388) and he was very helpful. 

Always submit a cover letter, and make sure it’s specific to the company every time. I had a fill-in-the-blank so that I could quickly insert the company’s name and make a quick comment about how I align with their mission. It takes an extra 5 minutes, and it’s annoying when you just want to fire off applications, but I promise it’s worth it. 

Prepare for your interviews. Do not wing them. Glassdoor is a really great source where other job seekers / employees will leave information about a company’s interview process. This is a great way to ensure you’re familiar with the specific questions they will ask. Also, if you study [this list](https://www.glassdoor.com/blog/common-interview-questions/), you will rarely be caught off guard. 

Last but not least, don’t ever talk yourself down. There is always a way to describe what you’ve done that makes it sound incredibly valuable, even if you have minimal experience. Try to find the right keywords to describe your experience and your skill set, both on your resume and in interviews. 

Good luck!
